meta.note: Values are rounded from public NASA/vendor fact sheets and sized for gameplay. Mark: verify each 'source' URL and adjust numbers before submission.

missions.name: Artemis Lunar South Pole Ice Scout
missions.tagline: Map water ice hiding in permanently shadowed craters.
missions.required_text: At least one instrument that detects hydrogen/water ice.
missions.brief: Artemis crews need to know where ice is before they land. Solar power is reduced by low sun angles at the pole. The Moon is close, so radio links are fast.

missions.name: Mars Methane Orbiter
missions.tagline: Hunt for trace gases that could point to geology or life.
missions.inspired_by: ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, MAVEN, MRO
missions.brief: Sunlight at Mars is under half of Earth's. Signals are slow: Mars is tens of millions of km away, so downlink rate falls with distance squared.

missions.name: Psyche Metal Asteroid
missions.tagline: Visit a world that may be an exposed planetary core.
missions.required_text: One composition instrument AND one magnetometer.
missions.brief: At about 2.9 AU sunlight is roughly 12% of Earth's. The delta-v to arrive and orbit is large, and the link is weak and shared on the Deep Space Network.

instruments.name: Neutron Detector (LEND-class)
instruments.blurb: Neutrons escaping the surface are fewer where hydrogen (water ice) is buried.

instruments.name: UV Spectrograph (LAMP-class)
instruments.blurb: Sees surface frost in permanently dark craters using starlight.

instruments.name: Thermal Radiometer (Diviner-class)
instruments.blurb: Finds the coldest places where ice can survive for billions of years.

instruments.name: Laser Altimeter (LOLA-class)
instruments.blurb: Builds precise terrain maps for landing-site safety.

instruments.name: Imaging Radar (Mini-RF-class)
instruments.blurb: Radar returns can hint at ice layers under the surface.

instruments.name: Trace-Gas Spectrometer (NOMAD-class)
instruments.blurb: Detects methane at parts-per-billion by watching sunlight through the atmosphere.

instruments.name: Atmospheric Chemistry Suite (ACS-class)
instruments.blurb: Three infrared channels that measure methane, water and aerosols.

instruments.name: Neutral Gas Mass Spectrometer (NGIMS-class)
instruments.blurb: Samples the upper atmosphere to study how Mars lost its air.

instruments.name: Imaging Spectrometer (CRISM-class)
instruments.blurb: Maps minerals that formed in water.

instruments.name: High-Res Camera (HiRISE-class)
instruments.blurb: Spectacular images, but very hungry for downlink bandwidth.

instruments.name: Gamma-Ray & Neutron Spectrometer (GRNS-class)
instruments.blurb: Reads the elements on the surface: iron, nickel, and more.

instruments.name: Magnetometer (boom-mounted)
instruments.blurb: A remnant magnetic field would be strong evidence of a former core.

instruments.name: Multispectral Imager (twin cameras)
instruments.blurb: Shape, geology and surface color of the asteroid.

instruments.name: Radio Science (gravity mapping)
instruments.blurb: Tracks tiny changes in the radio signal to weigh the asteroid.

tooltips.mass: Launch vehicles can only throw so much mass toward each destination. Every kilogram of fuel, instrument, or structure counts.
tooltips.power: Solar arrays collect less light the farther you go from the Sun (inverse square law). Instruments and the bus must stay under what the arrays produce.
tooltips.budget: Development plus launch cost must stay under the mission cost ceiling. Cheap rockets limit mass, expensive rockets limit budget.
tooltips.data: Instruments create data every day. The onboard recorder must hold it until the next contact with Earth.
tooltips.comms: Downlink rate drops with the square of distance, and Deep Space Network time is shared. If you make more data than you can send, science is lost.
tooltips.time: Everything must be built before the launch window closes. A missed window means waiting months or years for planets to line up again.
